overview: Alemanni, also written Alamanni or Alamans, names groups associated with the Upper Rhine and southwestern Germany in late antiquity. Early descriptions come from Roman outsiders. Historians do not treat them as one unchanged migrating people or assume that a single king governed every community.

periods.title: Communities beside the Roman frontier
periods.summary: Different groups settled in former Roman territory east of the Rhine during the third and fourth centuries. Roman writers grouped them under the Alemannic name. Regional rulers could negotiate separately with Rome and with one another.

periods.title: Frankish victories and Ostrogothic protection
periods.summary: Frankish victories around 500 curtailed independent rulers, although the sequence and dates are debated. Some leaders came under Ostrogothic protection. The Ostrogoths transferred their Alemannic territories to the Franks in 536 to 537.

periods.title: Alemannia within the Frankish realm
periods.summary: Dukes governed within the Frankish political world while local identities and law continued. Increasingly hereditary ducal power met Carolingian opposition. The defeat of resistance at Cannstatt in 746 brought stronger integration under Frankish counts.

items.text: At Vörstetten’s Grub site, excavated building traces informed the museum’s reconstruction of a house combining living and livestock areas. Its timber posts and clay-coated wattle walls make the work of construction understandable. The standing museum building is a modern interpretation of archaeological evidence, not a surviving ancient house.

Circular marks in the settlement soil suggested a round well shaft. They did not establish whether its lining used boards or woven willow. The museum therefore distinguishes the excavated indication of water supply from choices made in rebuilding the well. Preserved traces do not always determine every construction detail.

Iron-ore fragments and smelting slag found at Vörstetten document local iron production. The museum interprets one building plan as a possible smithy, but keeps that attribution tentative. Slag is evidence of a manufacturing process; assigning that process to a particular building requires an additional argument.

A beechwood bed from grave 27 at Lauchheim-Mittelhofen is dated to 703 to 704. Pegged joints, a stabilizing wedge and traces of leather and plant-fiber padding suggest use for sleeping. Added end boards converted it for burial. The object connects skilled joinery, household comfort and funerary reuse.

A maple flask from Trossingen grave 58, dated around 580, was hollowed on a lathe and closed with a separate plate sealed with resin. Its suspension loops and standing base allowed different uses. Beer remains survived inside, linking woodworking techniques with the handling of drink.

The lyre from the same grave is cataloged around 560. Its pegs indicate six strings; the strings themselves are missing. Playing wear, replaced pegs and small repair nails show continued use and maintenance. Charcoal emphasized engraved decoration, joining musical function with visual craftsmanship. Its maker and repertoire remain unidentified.

sections.title: Settlements, households and the evidence of graves

items.text: At Lauchheim-Mittelhofen, archaeologists investigated settlement remains dating from the sixth through eleventh centuries, close to the Wasserfurche cemetery. Ground-level building plans and sunken structures provide evidence beyond grave gifts. They reveal where people built and worked, helping balance the prominence of elite objects in museum collections.

The Mittelhofen project compares settlement plans with cemetery records to investigate social and economic organization. Such comparison matters because a lavish burial describes a particular treatment of the dead, while houses record another part of community life. Neither evidence alone supplies a complete picture of every household.

Niederstotzingen’s burial ground, used roughly from 580 to 630, contained weapons, armor and horse equipment associated with several distant regions. A 2018 genetic study identified close relatives among people buried with differently associated goods. Object style therefore cannot simply be read as the wearer’s ancestry or place of birth.

The same study found people without detectable close kinship buried alongside relatives. Its authors interpreted the group through both family relationships and fellowship. They also cautioned that this richly furnished, predominantly male burial group was not representative of the wider population. A small cemetery cannot stand for all Alemannic society.

Geuenich emphasizes that the early name is preserved in outsiders’ accounts. Similar pottery and other objects can demonstrate connections between regions without proving that all their users shared one identity. The formation of Alemannic communities was a process, not a securely documented founding ceremony or a single migration.

Alemannic legal texts distinguish free, dependent and unfree people and describe courts and offices. Their categories do not map automatically onto richly or poorly furnished graves. Written rules and burial evidence answer different questions about rank, rights and power.

ending.text: Frankish control developed through victories around 500, acquisition of Ostrogothic territories in 536 to 537, and the suppression of resistance at Cannstatt in 746. The last event strengthened Carolingian control within the Frankish realm. It ended a phase of political autonomy, not the lives or identity of the region’s communities.
